lead: A lubricant is not chosen by feel. It is chosen by measured properties: how its viscosity changes with temperature, how cold it can pour, how hot it can safely be, how it resists oxidation and what additives it carries. These properties decide whether oil reaches the bearings at a cold start, stays on the cylinder wall at full load, and keeps sludge and wear low over thousands of kilometres. This chapter lists those properties with units and explains how additives turn a base oil into an engine oil.
prereq: You need Lubrication systems and engine friction for where the oil goes and what it must do at each sliding pair.

blocks.text: Viscosity is the oil's resistance to shear. Dynamic viscosity μ (Greek mu) is shear stress divided by shear rate; its SI unit is the pascal second (Pa·s), and engine oils are quoted in millipascal seconds (mPa·s). Kinematic viscosity ν (Greek nu) is μ divided by density; its unit is mm²/s, also called the centistoke (cSt). A grade such as 10W-40 is set by the SAE (Society of Automotive Engineers) J300 limits, not by one number. The W means winter. The 10W part fixes low-temperature limits, a maximum cold-cranking viscosity and a maximum pumping viscosity at stated sub-zero temperatures, plus a minimum kinematic viscosity at 100 °C. The 40 part fixes a kinematic-viscosity band at 100 °C, 12.5 to below 16.3 mm²/s, and a minimum high-temperature high-shear viscosity at 150 °C. A multigrade oil meets both sets of limits. Its viscosity index (VI) is a dimensionless number showing how flat the viscosity-temperature curve is: a high VI means little thinning when hot. Pour point is the lowest temperature at which the oil still moves, in °C. Cloud point is the temperature at which wax first makes the oil cloudy, in °C. Flash point is the lowest temperature at which vapour above the oil ignites under test, in °C. Fire point is the higher temperature at which the vapour keeps burning for about five seconds, usually 10–20 °C above flash point.

Carbon residue is the mass percent of coke left when oil is heated without air; it warns about deposits in hot zones. Acidity is measured as total acid number (TAN) in mg KOH per gram of oil. The base reserve is total base number (TBN), also in mg KOH/g. TAN rises as oil oxidises; TBN falls as it neutralises acids. Oxidation stability is the time or temperature needed to reach a chosen TAN, sludge or viscosity rise; it has no single unit. Oiliness is the ability to lower friction in boundary lubrication, where surfaces touch through a very thin film; it is judged on friction rigs, not by a simple number. Emulsification is the tendency to hold water; demulsibility is the reverse, stated as time to separate or percent water separated. Foaming is air held in the oil; it is reported as foam volume in mL and collapse time in seconds. Foam reduces oil flow and can cause cavitation in the pump.

Additives are 1–20 percent by mass of the finished oil. A viscosity index improver is a polymer that coils when cold and expands when hot, so it raises hot viscosity more than cold viscosity; this is how a 10W base oil becomes a 10W-40. Antioxidants break the chain reaction that forms acids and sludge. Detergents keep hot metal clean and neutralise acids. Dispersants keep soot and sludge suspended so they drain out instead of sticking. Anti-wear agents form a film on loaded surfaces; extreme-pressure (EP) agents react under high pressure to stop seizure. Corrosion and rust inhibitors coat metal with a thin film. Pour point depressants stop wax crystals from joining into a gel. Antifoam agents, often silicone, break bubbles. The base oil still carries the load. Most additives change its chemistry and its surface behaviour; the VI improver and the pour point depressant are the two that change how it flows.

sections.h3: Oil consumption and its fraction of fuel

blocks.text: Oil leaves an engine by four main routes. Ring blow-by pushes oil mist past the rings. Worn valve guides pull oil into the inlet. Turbo seals and crankcase ventilation can carry oil vapour. Volatility boils light oil fractions at high temperature. Consumption is best stated as a fraction of fuel used: f = V<sub>oil</sub> ÷ V<sub>fuel</sub>, where V<sub>oil</sub> is the oil added in litres and V<sub>fuel</sub> is the fuel burnt in litres. If distance D is in km and fuel economy FE is in km per litre, V<sub>fuel</sub> = D ÷ FE. A good road engine stays below 1 percent; worn or racing engines can reach about 2 percent.
f is the oil consumption fraction, dimensionless; V<sub>oil</sub> is the oil added in litres; V<sub>fuel</sub> is the fuel burnt in litres; D is distance in km; FE is fuel economy in km per litre.

examples.question: A car covers 1000 km and its owner tops up 0.4 litre of engine oil. Fuel average is 15 km per litre. Find the fuel used, the oil consumption as a fraction of fuel, and the same value as a percentage.
steps: Fuel used V<sub>fuel</sub> = D ÷ FE = 1000 km ÷ 15 km/L = 66.7 L.
Oil fraction f = V<sub>oil</sub> ÷ V<sub>fuel</sub> = 0.4 L ÷ 66.7 L = 0.006.
examples.answer: Fuel used is 66.7 L; oil consumption is 0.006 of fuel, that is 0.6 percent.

examples.question: A used-oil laboratory measures an engine oil at 100 °C: dynamic viscosity 12.0 mPa·s and density 0.84 g/cm³ (840 kg/m³). Find its kinematic viscosity in mm²/s and say which SAE hot grade band it falls in. The bands at 100 °C are: 30, 9.3 to below 12.5; 40, 12.5 to below 16.3; 50, 16.3 to below 21.9 mm²/s.
steps: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density: ν = μ ÷ ρ.
In SI units: μ = 12.0 mPa·s = 0.0120 Pa·s; ρ = 840 kg/m³.
Since 1 mm²/s = 10⁻⁶ m²/s, ν = 14.3 mm²/s (14.3 cSt). A quick route: mPa·s divided by g/cm³ gives mm²/s directly, 12.0 ÷ 0.84 = 14.3.
14.3 lies between 12.5 and 16.3, so the oil is still in the 40 band. If fuel dilution thinned it below 12.5 mm²/s it would have fallen to a 30, a common reason to change oil early.
examples.answer: ν = 14.3 mm²/s, inside the SAE 40 band at 100 °C.

traps: A higher viscosity grade is not automatically better. Too thick an oil starves narrow passages at cold start and raises churning loss; match the grade to ambient temperature and engine design.
The W in 10W-40 means winter, not weight. 10W-40 is one oil that meets a cold 10W limit and a hot 40 band, not a mixture of grade 10 and grade 40.
Flash point is not fire point and neither is autoignition temperature. Fire point is higher, and a high flash point alone does not prove good lubrication.
TAN and TBN use the same unit, mg KOH/g, but move in opposite directions. Rising TAN and falling TBN both mean the oil is ageing.
Pour point is not the lowest safe operating temperature. Oil can still pour but be far too thick to pump or protect bearings.

quiz.q: Define viscosity index and give its unit.
quiz.a: Viscosity index is a dimensionless measure of how little an oil's viscosity changes with temperature; higher VI means a flatter curve.

quiz.q: What does the W in 10W-40 mean?
quiz.a: Winter. The 10W part sets low-temperature limits (cold cranking and pumping); the 40 part sets the kinematic-viscosity band at 100 °C, 12.5 to below 16.3 mm²/s, with a high-shear minimum at 150 °C.

quiz.q: Why does a multigrade oil use a VI improver?
quiz.a: The polymer expands when hot, raising hot viscosity more than cold viscosity, so one oil meets both the cold 10W and hot 40 limits.

quiz.q: An engine adds 0.35 L oil while burning 50 L fuel. Find oil consumption as a percentage of fuel.
Give one difference between a detergent and a dispersant.
quiz.a: A detergent keeps hot metal clean and neutralises acids; a dispersant keeps soot and sludge suspended in the oil.

quiz.q: A 20W-50 oil is used in a cold climate. Give two problems.
quiz.a: The 20W cold limit is too thick for easy cranking and fast oil flow, so startup wear rises; thicker oil also raises churning loss and can starve narrow passages before warm-up.

quiz.q: Why is oil consumption stated as a fraction of fuel, not only as litres per 1000 km?
quiz.a: Fuel burnt measures the work the engine did and so the blow-by and heat that drove the oil loss. A truck and a scooter may both use 0.5 L per 1000 km, yet the truck burns far more fuel, so its fraction is much smaller and its engine healthier. The fraction compares oil loss with the duty that caused it.

quiz.q: Name two additives that protect surfaces.

beyond: In industry, oil choice is tied to maker specifications and standard engine tests for oxidation, wear and deposits. Low-viscosity oils such as 0W-16 and 0W-20 serve fuel economy, while phosphorus and sulphur limits protect catalytic converters. Search for API and ACEA oil sequences, base-oil groups and used-oil analysis.
